## Buoy A01

<!-- add the photo as dashboard/img/buoy.jpg, then uncomment this line:
![Buoy A01 in Massachusetts Bay](img/buoy.jpg){fig-alt="Photo of buoy A01" width=70% fig-align="center"}
-->

BloomBoard forecasts chlorophyll at **buoy A01**, a moored ocean observing
platform in Massachusetts Bay (about 42.52°N, 70.57°W) in roughly 65m of
water. The buoy is owned and operated by the University of Maine and is part
of the Gulf of Maine Ocean Array run by the Northeastern Regional Association
of Coastal Ocean Observing Systems (NERACOOS).

## What it measures

Sensors on the buoy and along its mooring line record weather above the water
and conditions at several depths below it. BloomBoard uses:

- chlorophyll fluorescence at 3m
- water temperature, salinity, and conductivity at 1m and 20m
- water temperature at 51m
- air temperature

Readings arrive many times a day and are averaged to one value per day for the
forecast.

## Who uses it and why

- **Mariners**: boaters, fishermen, surfers, and pilots check buoy winds,
  waves, and temperatures every day before heading out.
- **Researchers**: the buoy's subsurface temperature, salinity, oxygen,
  and biological measurements are a long record of how the Gulf of Maine
  changes through the seasons and from year to year.
- **Water-quality managers**: monitoring programs in Massachusetts Bay,
  including the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority (MWRA), track
  conditions in the bay.

## Why forecast chlorophyll

Chlorophyll is a measure of phytoplankton, the microscopic algae at the base of
the ocean food web. When phytoplankton grow quickly into a bloom, they change
water clarity and oxygen and the food available to fish and shellfish, and some
blooms can be harmful. A forecast of when a bloom will peak and fade gives the
people watching these waters a few days of notice. See the
[Documentation](documentation.qmd) page for how the forecast works.
